families.family: requirement strings with a large number of extra markers (extras), which produce many Token objects during tokenization; the added __slots__ on Token reduces per‑token memory and attribute‑access cost, so this path should become faster.
families.why: The tokenizer creates one Token per extra name (plus a few for the name, specifier, URL, marker). With many extras the number of Token allocations dominates runtime, and __slots__ eliminates the per‑instance __dict__, giving a measurable speedup.
families.size_meaning: n = number of extras in the requirement (each extra adds a token).
families.make_source:
def make(n):
    # Build a requirement like  pkg[extra0,extra1,...,extraN-1] >=1.0
    extras = ','.join(f'extra{i}' for i in range(n))
    req = f'pkg[{extras}] >=1.0'
    return [[req]]

families.why: Long requirement strings with many extras, version specifiers, a URL and an environment marker exercise the tokenizer heavily; the added __slots__ on Token and Tokenizer reduces per‑token attribute‑access overhead, so this family should be faster in head.
families.size_meaning: n = number of extra names (also drives length of specifier and marker)
families.make_source:
def make(n):
    # Build a requirement with n extras, a multi‑clause specifier, a URL and a marker.
    extras = ','.join(f'extra{i}' for i in range(n))
    specifier = '>=1.0,<2.0,!=1.5,==1.2.*'
    url = 'https://example.com/pkg'
    marker = 'python_version>="3.6" and sys_platform=="linux"'
    req = f'myproj[{extras}]{specifier} @ {url} ; {marker}'
    return [[req]]

families.why: A single, well‑formed requirement like "requests>=2.25" exercises the fast path of the tokenizer (few tokens, no extras, no markers). Adding __slots__ to Token/Tokenizer reduces per‑token overhead, so this case should be faster in the head version.
families.size_meaning: Number of characters in the version specifier; grows linearly with n.
families.make_source:
def make(n: int):
    # n controls the length of the version number (e.g. 1.0, 1.0.0, …)
    # keep it a valid PEP 440 version.
    base = "requests>="
    # produce versions like 1.0, 1.0.0, 1.0.0.0 …
    version = ".".join(str(i) for i in range(1, n + 2))
    req = base + version
    return [[req]]

families.family: a batch of very small, trivial requirements (just a plain project name). Each call constructs a fresh Tokenizer instance; the __slots__ version adds a tiny per‑instance overhead for slot initialization that can outweigh the saved __dict__ when the token stream is only one or two tokens.
families.why: Tokenizer.__init__ now has to allocate the fixed slot array for every parse. When the input yields only a single token, the fixed cost of slot setup dominates, making the new version slightly slower per call.
families.size_meaning: n = number of separate tiny requirements (capped at 8 because the generator returns at most 8 argument lists).
families.make_source:
def make(n):
    # Produce up to 8 independent tiny requirements; each is a separate call.
    count = min(8, max(1, n))
    return [[f'pkg{i}'] for i in range(count)]

families.why: A minimal requirement ('pkg') creates only a handful of Token objects. The extra class‑level __slots__ descriptor look‑ups add a constant overhead per object creation that can dominate when the workload is tiny, making head slightly slower for very small inputs.
families.size_meaning: n = number of independent tiny requirements parsed in one batch

families.why: Each extra (e.g. "[extra1,extra2,…]") is tokenized as a separate identifier token. A requirement with many extras creates many Token objects; the new __slots__ layout may add a small per‑object allocation cost that outweighs the attribute‑access win when the token count is high.
families.size_meaning: Number of extras in the requirement; token count grows O(n).
families.make_source:
def make(n: int):
    # Build a name with n extras: pkg[extra0,extra1,…,extra{n‑1}]
    extras = ",".join(f"extra{i}" for i in range(n))
    req = f"pkg[{extras}]"
    return [[req]]
